title: Unum's Third-Quarter Adjusted Operating Income Falls 27% to $349 Million as Group Disability Earnings Drop 60% on Elevated Claim Submissions, While a $853 Million Investment Loss Pushes Net Income Into the Red
summary: Unum Group reported a third-quarter 2026 net loss of $419.7 million and adjusted operating income of $349.0 million, down from $479.4 million, as group disability earnings fell 60% on a 67.1% benefit ratio, while Colonial Life earnings rose 35% and the company bought back $202 million of stock and guided full-year adjusted operating income to $8.30 to $8.50 per share.
description:
Unum Group released its third-quarter 2026 results on November 3, 2026, with a conference call the following morning. The release is built around a gap between two measures. The net result was a loss of $419.7 million, while the company's adjusted operating income, which it uses to describe underlying performance, was a profit of $349.0 million. Both were weaker than a year earlier. This article reports the figures from Unum's earnings release, filed as an exhibit to a current report with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, and notes where a number has been calculated here rather than reported.

A change in how earnings are defined

Before the figures, one caution. The release says that adjusted operating income now excludes the results of the Closed Block, Unum's legacy business, and includes the annual reserve assumption updates. Prior periods were restated on that basis, so the comparisons in the release use the new definition. Readers who compare these numbers with Unum's earlier published figures may find differences for that reason. The third-quarter 2026 figure includes a net reserve decrease worth $0.33 per share.

The headline figures

Unum reported a net loss of $419.7 million, or $2.65 per diluted share, against net income of $39.7 million, or $0.23, in the third quarter of 2025. The release attributes the swing to net investment results: a pre-tax net investment loss of $853.0 million, against a gain of $128.0 million a year earlier. It says the loss mainly reflected impairments related to Fortitude Re. The Closed Block, which sits outside adjusted operating income, reported an adjusted operating loss of $135.6 million against a loss of $682.3 million.

After-tax adjusted operating income was $349.0 million, or $2.20 per share, against $479.4 million, or $2.81. That is a decline of about 27% in dollars and about 22% per share, calculated here. For the first nine months of the year, adjusted operating income was $1,047.5 million, or $6.56 per share, against $1,188.4 million, or $6.81. The effective tax rate on adjusted operating income was 20.5%, against 21.3%.

Premiums grew despite the weaker earnings. Total premium income was $2,800.7 million, up 4.2% from $2,688.0 million, and core operations premium growth was 4.7% at constant currency.

Where the earnings fell

Unum US, the largest segment, earned $315.3 million, down 35.2% from $486.8 million, even though premium rose 5.2% to $1,846.6 million and net investment income rose 8.6% to $164.9 million. Sales were $163.9 million, down 8.5%.

The pressure was concentrated in group disability. Its operating income fell 60.4% to $94.8 million from $239.3 million. Premium was up 4.0% to $816.6 million, but the benefit ratio, which measures claims relative to premium, was 67.1% against 47.8%. Group life and accidental death and dismemberment earned $78.2 million, down 14.3%, with a benefit ratio of 68.8% against 65.4%. Supplemental and voluntary earned $142.3 million, down 9.0%, with a benefit ratio of 45.4% against 40.3%.

Unum International earned just $0.2 million, against $44.2 million. Its sales fell 41.6% to $29.0 million, and its benefit ratio rose to 86.3% from 69.4%. Within it, Unum UK recorded an adjusted operating loss of 1.4 million pounds, against income of 27.0 million pounds, with a benefit ratio of 91.0% against 73.4%. The release gives these figures but, in the portion reviewed, no explanation for the UK result.

Colonial Life was the bright spot. It earned $169.4 million, up 35.0% from $125.5 million, on premium of $470.0 million, up 3.0%. Its benefit ratio improved to 38.0% from 46.3%, and sales rose 6.4% to $132.6 million. The Corporate segment lost $45.7 million against $47.7 million. Adding the four operating segments gives $439.2 million before tax, calculated here, which is consistent with the after-tax total once the 20.5% tax rate is applied.

Management's explanation

Chief executive Richard McKenney said: "Our underlying earnings results did fall short of our expectations," and attributed the shortfall to "elevated claim submissions in group disability." The release does not, in the portion reviewed, say how long the company expects the higher submission rate to last.

Capital and shareholder returns

Unum estimated its weighted-average risk-based capital ratio for its traditional U.S. insurers at about 485%, and holding company liquidity at $1,383.4 million. In the quarter it repurchased about 2.1 million shares for roughly $202.0 million and paid common dividends of $80.1 million. Year-to-date capital returned was $1,038.5 million. Shares outstanding were 156.2 million at September 30, 2026, against about 169.0 million a year earlier, a reduction of about 7.5% calculated here.

Book value per share was $68.90, up 6.7% from $64.56. Excluding accumulated other comprehensive income, it was $76.73, down 0.9% from $77.39. Adjusted operating return on equity for core operations was 21.3%.

Guidance

For the full year 2026, Unum expects adjusted operating income of $8.30 to $8.50 per share, including about $0.33 from the third-quarter reserve item. The nine-month figure of $6.56 implies that the fourth quarter would need to contribute roughly $1.74 to $1.94 per share to reach that range, calculated here. The release does not state how the company expects to get there, and this article does not forecast.

What to watch

Three things stand out. The first is the benefit ratio in group disability, which moved by nearly twenty percentage points in a year. The second is the contrast between that business and Colonial Life, which shows that the weakness is specific to certain lines. The third is the investment loss tied to Fortitude Re, which affected net income but not adjusted operating income. Anyone relying on these figures should read the full exhibit, which contains the reconciliations between the measures.
source_name: Unum Group (third-quarter 2026 earnings release, Exhibit 99.1 to Form 8-K, released November 3, 2026)
image_alt: Financial documents and calculator representing an insurer's quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Unum reported a net loss of $419.7 million, or $2.65 per diluted share, against net income of $39.7 million a year earlier, because net investment losses of $853.0 million, mainly impairments related to Fortitude Re, replaced a $128.0 million gain.

After-tax adjusted operating income was $349.0 million, or $2.20 per share, against $479.4 million, or $2.81, a decline of about 27% calculated here, on a new definition that excludes the Closed Block and includes annual reserve assumption updates.

Group disability operating income fell 60.4% to $94.8 million as its benefit ratio rose to 67.1% from 47.8%, and chief executive Richard McKenney said results fell short because of elevated claim submissions in group disability.

Colonial Life income rose 35.0% to $169.4 million and its benefit ratio improved to 38.0% from 46.3%, while Unum International income fell to $0.2 million and Unum UK moved to an adjusted operating loss of 1.4 million pounds.
Unum guided full-year 2026 adjusted operating income to $8.30 to $8.50 per share, repurchased about $202.0 million of stock in the quarter, and estimated a risk-based capital ratio near 485%.
why_it_matters: Unum is one of the largest US sellers of disability, life and supplemental benefits through employers, so a sharp rise in disability claim costs matters to employers who buy the cover and to investors who track the sector. The quarter also shows how a change in how an insurer defines its headline earnings can complicate year-on-year comparisons.

title: Genworth's Third-Quarter Loss of $41 Million Reflects a Deeper Long-Term Care Statutory Loss, While Enact Earns $132 Million and the Company Authorises a New $500 Million Buyback
summary: Genworth Financial reported a third-quarter 2026 net loss of $41 million, or $0.11 per share, against income of $116 million, with adjusted operating income excluding the Closed Block at $102 million, Enact earning $132 million, a legacy-insurer risk-based capital ratio of 274%, and a new $500 million share repurchase authorisation.
description:
Genworth Financial, Inc. released its third-quarter 2026 results on November 4, 2026, with a conference call on November 5. The company reported a net loss, a lower adjusted operating result excluding its legacy Closed Block, a steady contribution from its mortgage insurance subsidiary Enact and a deterioration in the statutory results of its long-term care business. It also announced a larger share repurchase authorisation. This article reports the figures from the earnings release filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, noting that some capital figures are company estimates because statutory statements were not final when the release was issued.

Headline results

Net loss available to common stockholders was $41 million, or $0.11 per diluted share. A year earlier the company reported net income of $116 million, or $0.28 per share, and in the second quarter of 2026 it reported $47 million, or $0.12. Diluted weighted-average shares were 375.5 million, down from 413.3 million a year earlier, a reduction of about 9% calculated here.

Adjusted operating income excluding the Closed Block, the measure that best reflects the ongoing business, was $102 million, or $0.27 per share, against $113 million, or $0.28, and $112 million, or $0.29, in the second quarter. Total adjusted operating income, which includes the Closed Block, was a loss of $44 million, against income of $17 million a year earlier and $2 million in the second quarter. Net investment losses reduced net income by $9 million, against gains of $78 million in the year-earlier quarter, which helps explain why net income moved so far from adjusted operating income.

Segments

Enact earned $132 million, against $134 million a year earlier and $143 million in the second quarter. Corporate and Other lost $30 million, against $21 million. The Closed Block lost $146 million, against $96 million a year earlier and $110 million in the second quarter.

The Closed Block's actual-versus-expected losses were $111 million before tax, against $127 million in the second quarter and $100 million a year earlier. The release attributes the main drivers to lower terminations, mostly from mortality, and higher long-term care benefit utilisation. In plain terms, policyholders were living longer or using benefits more than the company had assumed.

Legacy insurers

Genworth does not report long-term care, life and annuities as separate segments. They appear instead as statutory pre-tax results of the legacy insurers. Long-term care was a loss of $151 million, against a loss of $75 million a year earlier and $82 million in the second quarter. Life was a loss of $31 million, against $2 million and $22 million. Annuities earned $39 million, against $65 million and $110 million. The total statutory pre-tax result was a loss of $143 million, against a loss of $12 million a year earlier and a gain of $6 million in the second quarter.

The release says long-term care results continued to benefit from premium increases and benefit reductions under its in-force rate actions, with an estimated net present value of about $35.0 billion achieved since 2012. It does not, in the portion reviewed, explain the doubling of the quarterly statutory loss beyond the experience drivers described above.

Enact

Enact's primary new insurance written was $14.1 billion, against $14.0 billion a year earlier and $15.2 billion in the second quarter. The company attributes the 7% sequential decline to higher mortgage rates. Primary insurance in force was $275.1 billion, up about 1%. The loss ratio was 20%, against 15% a year earlier and 14% in the second quarter, and the pre-tax reserve release was $37 million, against $45 million. Pre-tax net investment income was $74 million, against $68 million.

Enact's equity was $4.21 billion, against $4.32 billion. Its PMIERs sufficiency ratio, the regulatory measure of capital against requirements for private mortgage insurers, was 158% against 162%, with $1.83 billion above requirements. Enact paid a quarterly dividend of $0.24 per share and entered into a quota share reinsurance agreement covering the 2028 book year. Genworth received $122 million of Enact capital returns at the holding level.

Capital and liquidity

The estimated risk-based capital ratio for the legacy insurance companies on a consolidated basis was 274%, down from 303% a year earlier and 286% in the second quarter. The company notes that RBC and PMIERs figures are estimates. Net investment income, net of taxes, was $603 million, down from $631 million a year earlier and $660 million in the second quarter.

Genworth Holdings had cash and liquid assets of $320 million, up from $254 million a year earlier and $215 million in the second quarter, with about $200 million held for future obligations. Outflows in the quarter included $80 million for share repurchases, $21 million to repurchase holding company debt at a discount and $6 million of debt service. Holding company debt principal fell by $21 million in the quarter.

Share repurchases

Genworth repurchased $80 million of its shares in the quarter at an average price of $10.05. Year to date it has repurchased $208 million at an average of $9.16, and since the programme began it has repurchased $998 million at an average of $6.66. The company announced a new $500 million authorisation. The release does not state a timetable for using it.

Management commentary

Chief executive Tom McInerney said Genworth "will be well positioned to drive sustainable long-term growth" as it executes its strategy. The portion of the release reviewed does not provide numerical guidance.

Reading the quarter

The picture is of two businesses moving in different directions. Enact remains profitable and well capitalised against its regulatory requirement, though its loss ratio rose. The legacy insurers lost more on long-term care and their capital ratio fell by 29 points over the year, calculated here. Share buybacks continued, and the holding company's reported cash inflow in the quarter was the $122 million of Enact capital returns. Policyholders should note that the RBC figure applies to the legacy insurers that issue their policies, while investors should note that the company's own adjusted measure excludes the Closed Block losses.
source_name: Genworth Financial, Inc. (third-quarter 2026 earnings release, Form 8-K, released November 4, 2026)
image_alt: Charts and figures on a desk representing an insurer's quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Genworth reported a net loss to common stockholders of $41 million, or $0.11 per diluted share, against net income of $116 million, or $0.28, a year earlier and $47 million in the second quarter of 2026.
Adjusted operating income excluding the Closed Block was $102 million, or $0.27 per share, against $113 million, or $0.28, while total adjusted operating income was a loss of $44 million.
Enact, the mortgage insurance subsidiary, earned $132 million against $134 million, with a loss ratio of 20% against 15% and a PMIERs sufficiency ratio of 158%.

Long-term care statutory pre-tax results were a loss of $151 million against a loss of $75 million, and the legacy insurers' risk-based capital ratio was an estimated 274%, down from 303% a year earlier.
Genworth repurchased $80 million of stock in the quarter at an average $10.05 per share and announced a new $500 million repurchase authorisation.
why_it_matters: Genworth combines a profitable mortgage insurer with a legacy long-term care book that continues to lose money, so its results show how two very different businesses can pull in opposite directions. Long-term care policyholders and mortgage lenders both have an interest in how that balance develops.

title: Voya Financial's Third-Quarter Adjusted Operating Earnings Edge Up to $240 Million, or $2.60 a Share, as the Dividend Rises 21% to $0.57 and the Buyback Authorisation Grows by $500 Million
summary: Voya Financial reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted operating earnings of $240 million, or $2.60 per share, against $239 million and $2.45, with net income of $193 million, retirement client assets up 12% to $878 billion, a 21% dividend increase to $0.57 and a $500 million larger buyback authorisation.
description:
Voya Financial, Inc. announced its third-quarter 2026 results on November 2, 2026, with a conference call the next day. The headline is stability in earnings alongside stronger capital returns: adjusted operating earnings were essentially flat, while the company raised its dividend by 21% and increased its share repurchase authorisation. This article reports the figures from Voya's earnings press release, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, and notes where a figure has been calculated here rather than reported. The release uses the segment names Retirement, Investment Management and Employee Benefits, and gives no formal numerical guidance.

Headline earnings

Net income available to common shareholders was $193 million, or $2.09 per diluted share, against $176 million, or $1.80, in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted operating earnings, the after-tax measure that excludes certain items, were $240 million, or $2.60 per diluted share, against $239 million, or $2.45. Dollar earnings were almost unchanged, but earnings per share rose about 6% calculated here, which is consistent with a smaller share count, although the release portion reviewed does not state the share count.

Adjusted operating earnings before income taxes were $288 million against $290 million. Income before income taxes was $287 million against $307 million. Total revenues were $2,025 million against $2,128 million. The results included about $25 million of pre-tax severance expense, which the release places in Corporate.

Segment results

Retirement earned $266 million before tax against $261 million. On a trailing twelve-month basis, its net revenue was $2,437 million against $2,296 million, up 6%, while its adjusted operating margin was 37.8% against 39.8%. Revenue is growing, but the margin has narrowed by two points.

Investment Management earned $58 million, excluding the noncontrolling interest, against $62 million, which the release attributes mainly to lower investment capital income. Trailing twelve-month net revenue was $1,056 million against $1,010 million, up 5%, with a margin of 28.6%.

Employee Benefits earned $51 million against $47 million, and that figure includes a $12 million favourable annual assumption update. Trailing twelve-month net revenue was $1,099 million against $1,001 million, up 10%, and the margin was 11.4% against 6.0%. The total aggregate loss ratio improved to 74% from 78%. Annualised in-force premiums and fees were $3.5 billion, which the release says is lower than a year earlier. Stop-loss is listed within Employee Benefits as a benefit product, but the release does not report separate stop-loss results.

Corporate recorded a loss of $87 million, excluding the noncontrolling interest, against $80 million, including the severance expense. Adding the four segments as reported gives $288 million, calculated here, which matches adjusted operating earnings before income taxes.

Assets and flows

In Retirement, total client assets were $878 billion against $785 billion, an increase of 12%, and the business served 10.3 million participants. Investment Management assets under management were $363 billion against $366 billion. The release attributes the small decline to divestitures and a sub-advisor transition, nearly offset by positive net flows and market appreciation. Excluding those items, net inflows were $1.4 billion in the quarter. Assets under advisory were $62 billion against $54 billion, with net inflows of $1.5 billion, also excluding divested businesses.

Capital returns

Voya said it generated about $225 million of excess capital in the quarter, a conversion of more than 90% of after-tax adjusted operating earnings, and returned about $150 million to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. Excess capital at September 30 was about $250 million. A final $20 million payment on the OneAmerica transaction was made, completing that deal.

The board raised the quarterly common dividend by 21% to $0.57 per share, starting in the fourth quarter of 2026. That implies a previous quarterly dividend of about $0.47, calculated here. The share repurchase authorisation was increased by $500 million, on top of about $163 million of remaining capacity at September 30, so total capacity is about $663 million, calculated here.

Management commentary and outlook

Chief executive Heather Lavallee said "Voya delivered a strong third quarter," and that the dividend and buyback increases "underscore our confidence in Voya's ability to deliver sustained earnings growth." The release gives no formal outlook. It points to the "improvement we expected in the second half," supported by commercial momentum and margin gains.

What the numbers say

Three points stand out. First, earnings are steady, but the total includes a $12 million favourable update in Employee Benefits and about $25 million of severance in Corporate, so the headline hides movement in its components. Second, Retirement's assets are growing quickly, 12% in a year, but its margin is lower. Third, the capital return commitments are larger. The dividend and the larger authorisation depend on excess capital continuing to be generated, and the release reports about $250 million of excess capital at September 30. Readers who want the reconciliation between adjusted and GAAP figures should read the full release, which contains it.
source_name: Voya Financial, Inc. (third-quarter 2026 earnings press release, Form 8-K, announced November 2, 2026)

key_points: Adjusted operating earnings were $240 million, or $2.60 per diluted share, against $239 million, or $2.45, while net income available to common shareholders rose to $193 million, or $2.09 per share, from $176 million, or $1.80.

Retirement earned $266 million before tax against $261 million, Investment Management earned $58 million against $62 million, and Employee Benefits earned $51 million against $47 million, including a $12 million favourable annual assumption update.
Voya's total client assets in Retirement rose 12% to $878 billion, while Investment Management assets under management were $363 billion against $366 billion, with net inflows of $1.4 billion.

The company said it generated about $225 million of excess capital in the quarter, returned about $150 million to shareholders, raised its quarterly dividend 21% to $0.57 from the fourth quarter, and increased its buyback authorisation by $500 million.
Results included about $25 million of pre-tax severance expense, and the release provides no formal financial guidance.
why_it_matters: Voya manages workplace retirement plans for millions of Americans and sells employee benefits such as stop-loss and disability cover, so its results show how retirement assets, investment flows and benefit claims are shaping a large US provider. The dividend and buyback decisions also show how much capital it believes it can return.

title: Globe Life Cuts Its 2026 Earnings Guidance to $15.35 to $15.65 a Share After Medicare Supplement and Evry Losses at United American, While Third-Quarter Operating Income Edges Up 1% Per Share
summary: Globe Life reported third-quarter 2026 net operating income of $378.8 million, or $4.84 per share, up 1% per share, but lowered 2026 guidance to $15.35 to $15.65 because of a roughly $16 million underwriting loss at Evry and about $7 million of excess Medicare Supplement claims at United American, and raised its buyback guidance to $725 million to $775 million.
description:
Globe Life Inc. released its third-quarter 2026 results on October 21, 2026, with a conference call the next day. Premium grew and earnings per share edged up, but the company lowered its guidance for 2026, pointing to two specific problems at its United American health business. This article reports the figures from the earnings release filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The release as reviewed does not contain executive quotes or dividend information, and this article does not supply either.

Earnings

Net income was $361.1 million, or $4.62 per diluted share, against $387.8 million, or $4.73, in the third quarter of 2025, a decline of about 2% per share. Net operating income, the non-GAAP measure that excludes certain items, was $378.8 million, or $4.84 per share, against $394.2 million, or $4.81, an increase of 1% per share. Dollar earnings fell about 4%, calculated here, while per-share figures rose because diluted shares fell to 78.2 million from 82.0 million. For the nine months, diluted earnings per share were $11.64 against $10.77.

Net income return on equity was 19.7% for the nine months against 21.9%, and net operating income return on equity excluding accumulated other comprehensive income was 15.9% against 16.6%. Legal proceedings reduced net income by $6.8 million, or $0.09 per share, against $2.0 million, or $0.02. The release gives no details of specific cases and lists litigation and regulatory actions only as a general risk.

Premium and underwriting

Total premium rose 7% to $1,311.4 million from $1,231.0 million. Life premium was $864.6 million, up 2%, and 66% of the total. Health premium was $446.9 million, up 16%, and 34% of the total.

Insurance underwriting income was $481.8 million, or $6.16 per share, against $503.1 million, or $6.13: down 4% in total but flat per share. Life underwriting margin was $458.2 million, or 53% of premium, against $481.6 million, or 57%. Health underwriting margin was $115.6 million, or 26% of premium, against $108.4 million, or 28%. Administrative expenses were $95.2 million against $89.8 million, and the ratio to premium was unchanged at 7.3%.

Distribution channels

American Income's life premium rose 4% to $470.4 million and its life margin rose 3% to $268.5 million, but producing agents fell 7% to 11,331 from 12,230, and life net sales were flat at $96.6 million. Liberty National's life premium rose 4% to $102.0 million and its sales rose 7%, but its life margin fell 27% to $51.0 million, which management attributed mainly to fluctuations in assumption updates. Its producing agents rose 9% to 4,187. Family Heritage's health premium rose 8% to $128.6 million and its health margin rose 12% to $56.8 million. Direct to Consumer's life premium was little changed at $243.1 million.

United American, the problem unit

United American's health premium rose 29% to $219.3 million, and net sales nearly doubled, rising 95% to $47.7 million. Its health margin, though, was a loss of $6.4 million against income of $16.1 million. The company cited two items: an underwriting loss of roughly $16 million at Evry, and about $7 million of excess prior-period Medicare Supplement claims tied to a claims-processing delay at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). Together these two items total about $23 million, calculated here, which is larger than the $22.5 million swing in the unit's margin, calculated here, suggesting that the rest of the unit earned about as much as it did a year earlier. The release does not explain what Evry is in the portion reviewed, so this article does not describe it.

Investments and capital

Net investment income was $295.9 million, up 3%. Excess investment income was $37.9 million, or $0.49 per share, against $36.9 million, or $0.45. The fixed maturity yield was 5.33% against 5.26%. New fixed maturity purchases were $832.5 million at a 6.4% yield. Total investments were $19.6 billion, with fixed maturities at 86% of the total and 97% of those investment grade. Net unrealised losses on fixed maturities in accumulated other comprehensive income were $2.69 billion. The company says it holds no credit default swaps and does not lend securities.

Shareholders' equity was $6.62 billion against $5.69 billion, and excluding accumulated other comprehensive income it was $8.04 billion against $7.66 billion. Book value per share was $85.35, up 23%, and $103.62 excluding accumulated other comprehensive income, up 11%.

Buybacks

Globe Life repurchased 1.1 million shares for $185 million at an average price of $175.61 in the quarter. It raised its 2026 repurchase guidance to $725 million to $775 million, from $670 million to $700 million.

Guidance

The company lowered 2026 net operating income guidance to $15.35 to $15.65 per share, and management attributed the cut to the two United American items, not to a change in the core business. That attribution is the company's own, and the release does not provide independent evidence of it. It set 2027 guidance at $16.10 to $17.10, which the release describes as a 7.1% increase at the midpoint.

Reading the results

The quarter shows growth in premium and agents in some channels, a decline in agent count at the largest life channel, a narrower life margin, and a health business whose growth came with a loss. Whether the guidance cut proves to be temporary depends on facts the release cannot settle, including how quickly the Medicare Supplement claims normalise. Anyone using the figures should read the full release, including the reconciliation of net operating income to net income.
source_name: Globe Life Inc. (third-quarter 2026 earnings release, Form 8-K, released October 21, 2026)

key_points: Net operating income was $378.8 million, or $4.84 per diluted share, against $394.2 million, or $4.81, while net income was $361.1 million, or $4.62 per share, against $387.8 million, or $4.73.
Total premium rose 7% to $1,311.4 million, with health premium up 16% to $446.9 million and life premium up 2% to $864.6 million.

Life underwriting margin fell to 53% of premium from 57%, and United American's health margin swung to a loss of $6.4 million from income of $16.1 million on a roughly $16 million Evry loss and about $7 million of excess Medicare Supplement claims linked to a CMS processing delay.
The company lowered its 2026 net operating income guidance to $15.35 to $15.65 per share, blaming those two United American items, and set 2027 guidance at $16.10 to $17.10.
Globe Life repurchased 1.1 million shares for $185 million in the quarter and raised its 2026 buyback guidance to $725 million to $775 million from $670 million to $700 million.
why_it_matters: Globe Life sells life and supplemental health cover, largely to middle-income households, so its results show how a mid-sized insurer manages premium growth, agent recruitment and claims costs. A guidance cut tied to two identified items is a useful example of how insurers distinguish one-off problems from core performance.

title: Bank of England Raises Bank Rate to 4% in an 8-1 Vote, Its First Increase Since August 2023, as Inflation Reaches 3.5% and the Bank Projects About 5% by Mid-2027
summary: On November 5, 2026 the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4% in an 8-1 vote, with one member preferring 0.5 points, after CPI inflation rose to 3.5% in September, and Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the start of a long sequence of hikes.
description:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate on Thursday, November 5, 2026, lifting it by 0.25 percentage points from 3.75% to 4%. The decision, by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), ends a pause that included holds on July 30 and September 17. This article draws on the Bank's own Bank Rate page, a summary published by the Mortgage Talk Association on November 6 and MoneyWeek's live coverage of the decision. The Bank's page does not report the vote breakdown, so the voting details come from the two secondary sources, which agree with each other. The Bank's full minutes and Monetary Policy Report were not reviewed for this article.

The decision

The committee voted 8-1 for a quarter-point rise. One member, Catherine Mann, voted for a larger half-point rise, to 4.25%. The summary notes that two members, Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor, had previously favoured holding rates and backed the increase this time. The Mortgage Talk Association describes this as the first increase in Bank Rate since August 2023, a claim the Bank's own page, as reviewed, does not state directly. The Bank's next decision is due on December 17, 2026.

Inflation and the outlook

Consumer price inflation was 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August. The Bank expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027, then ease as the direct effects of higher energy prices fade. The reports describe the outlook as highly uncertain, depending on how long the Middle East conflict lasts and how far energy costs pass through to other prices and wages. The 5% figure is the committee's projection, not an outcome, and projections of this kind are revised as new data arrive.

Why the committee acted

The MTA summary lists several reasons. The inflation outlook has worsened since the July forecast because global energy prices are higher. UK economic activity has been more resilient than expected, and the labour market appears to be stabilising. Some measures of underlying inflation have stopped falling. The Bank is concerned that the slack currently in the economy may not be enough to prevent the energy shock from causing more persistent inflation.

It also notes that second-round effects, meaning knock-on increases in wages and prices, have been limited so far, though the Bank warns they can take time to appear. Firms have absorbed some costs through lower margins, and fixed-price contracts and hedging have delayed the impact, but the Bank says these buffers may be temporary. The summary describes the move as a "modest increase as insurance against the risk of more persistent inflation," reflecting broad support for a small step.

What the Governor said

Governor Andrew Bailey said: "Today's increase shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes." MoneyWeek also quotes Sanjay Raja of Deutsche Bank, who said: "we don't think this is the start of a long hiking cycle." The summary adds that Bailey said the rise should not be read as the start of a fixed series of increases and that future decisions will depend on energy prices, wages, business pricing and economic activity. Those are statements of intention, not commitments.

Mortgage borrowers

MoneyWeek reports, citing Moneyfacts, that a tracker mortgage of 250,000 pounds over 25 years would rise by about 37 pounds a month. Borrowers on standard variable rates will probably see repayments rise too, though more gradually than trackers. Fixed-rate borrowers see no immediate change, because their rate changes only when the deal ends. Some lenders had already priced the rise into fixed rates before the announcement, which means that new fixed-rate deals may not move much on the day.

The pattern of decisions

The Bank Rate page shows three decisions in 2026 within its table: a hold at 3.75% on July 30, a hold at 3.75% on September 17, and the rise to 4% on November 5. The page says it is not a complete list of 2026 decisions. One secondary source, Karmactive, reported that the September vote was 6-3 to hold with three members wanting a rise to 4%. This article has not verified that against the Bank's minutes, so treat it as unconfirmed. If correct, the move from a 6-3 hold to an 8-1 rise in two months shows how quickly the committee's balance shifted.

Other central banks

The MTA summary notes that the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve both held rates steady at their late-October meetings. The Bank of England therefore moved against the pattern of the other two large central banks mentioned.

What the sources do not say

The sources reviewed do not give the Bank's growth forecast or its projection for Bank Rate. They do not say how the rise will affect savings rates, insurers' investment returns, annuity pricing or pension scheme valuations, and this article does not speculate. Households with variable-rate borrowing should check with their lenders for the exact change to their payments.

title: RBA Lifts the Cash Rate to 4.85% in a 6-3 Vote, the Fifth Rise of 2026 and the Highest Since 2008, as Unemployment Reaches 4.7% and Home Values Sit 4.3% Below Their Peak
summary: On November 3, 2026 the Reserve Bank of Australia raised the cash rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.85% in a 6-3 board vote, its fifth increase of the year, saying inflation remains elevated and broadly based even as unemployment rose to 4.7% and home values fell, with mortgage repayments rising about 77 to 80 dollars a month per 500,000 dollars borrowed.
description:
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) raised its cash rate target by 0.25 percentage points to 4.85% on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, the day of the Melbourne Cup. It was the fifth increase of 2026 and took the rate to its highest level since 2008. This article draws on two news reports, from SBS News and savings.com.au, which agree on the rate, the vote and the main statements. The RBA's own statement was not retrieved, so its wording is quoted as reported. The reports differ on one detail, the monthly mortgage cost, which is noted below.

The decision and the vote

The board raised the rate from 4.60% to 4.85%. Six members voted to raise it and three voted to hold at 4.60%. SBS notes that the RBA does not disclose how individual members voted. A 6-3 split is narrower than a unanimous decision, and the dissenting votes indicate that a third of the board saw a case for pausing.

What the RBA said

The RBA statement, as quoted by SBS, said: "Inflation remains elevated and recent data indicate that it is broadly based." The board also said, according to savings.com.au, that "a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted."

The RBA now expects inflation to remain elevated through much of 2027 and to reach the top of its 2 to 3 percent target range only in late 2027. SBS reports that this is about three quarters later than previously forecast. Underlying inflation was 3.7% annually in September, according to savings.com.au, and the RBA expects it to stay above 3% through much of 2027.

At the same time, the RBA acknowledged weaker signs. As quoted by SBS, it said: "The economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly and the unemployment rate has risen." Unemployment reached 4.7% in September, its highest in five years.

Governor Michele Bullock

SBS reports that Governor Michele Bullock said the decision is "what's needed to get inflation down." She argued that the rate rises address domestic capacity pressures, not oil prices directly. This is her stated reasoning, and the reports do not provide independent evidence on how much of the inflation is domestic.

Mortgage costs

Two sets of estimates were reported. Canstar, cited by SBS, estimates that a 0.25-point rise adds about $77 a month on a $500,000 loan and about $153 on a $1 million loan, assuming the full rise is passed through. Across all five increases this year, a $500,000 loan costs about $380 more a month. Savings.com.au puts the rise on a $500,000 mortgage at about $80 a month. Neither report explains the difference, and each figure is an estimate that assumes the full rise is passed on.

For median-value homes, REA estimates the monthly increase at $154 in Sydney, $107 in Melbourne, $134 in Brisbane, $119 in Adelaide, $125 in Perth, $112 in Canberra, $97 in Hobart and $83 in Darwin. Actual changes will depend on each borrower's loan, rate and lender.

The housing market

REA data cited by SBS show home values 4.3% below their March peak. Cotality's Tim Lawless described the downturn as demand-driven and possibly record-breaking. The reports do not give a forecast for house prices.

What banks and commentators expected

SBS reports that ANZ forecast a hike and expects cuts to start around November 2027, while CommBank, Westpac and NAB also tipped a rise but expect cuts from around August 2027. In a Finder survey, 75% of experts expected a hike, but only 55% thought it was the right move. Bendigo Bank's David Robertson argued for a pause. These are forecasts and opinions, not decisions.

Politics

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the decision was widely expected but still difficult for households, and he flagged further budget savings in the December mid-year update. Angus Moore of realestate.com.au said higher mortgage costs will continue to weigh on household spending and slow economic growth.

What the reports do not say

The reports reviewed do not give the RBA's forecasts for growth or unemployment, do not describe the board's discussion beyond the statement, and do not say how the rise will affect savings rates, business lending or insurers. This article therefore makes no claim on those points. The inflation figures also deserve care: the 3.7% underlying rate comes from savings.com.au, while SBS focuses on the RBA's own description of inflation as elevated and broadly based, and the two reports do not give a headline inflation figure to compare it with.

What to watch

The split vote is the most important detail for what comes next, because it shows the board is not united. The bank forecasts quoted above place the first cuts in the second half of 2027, but the RBA itself has not said so, and the reports show it expects inflation to stay elevated for another year. Borrowers on variable rates should check their lender's notices for the exact change to their repayments, and those on fixed rates should note when their terms end.
